subdomainName: Control Physical and Logical Access to Assets
title: Access control matrix: ACLs vs. capability lists
prompt: In an access control matrix, which view is an ACL and which is a capability list?
answerSummary: Rows are subjects and columns are objects. A column read down (one object, all subjects) is an access control list attached to the object. A row read across (one subject, all objects) is a capability list held by the subject.
mnemonic: ACL = Attached to the object (Column). Capability = Carried by the subject (row).
examTrapWarning: Capability tables are tied to subjects, ACLs to objects. Questions often swap them.

columns.label: ACL
points: Lists every subject and its rights
Easy to see who can access a file

columns.label: Capability list
points: Lists every object the subject can access
Easy to see what a user can do

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Identification and Authentication of People, Devices, and Services
topicName: MFA Factors (Something You Know, Have, Are, Somewhere You Are)
title: Authentication factor types
prompt: Name the three main authentication factor types with examples, plus the two supplementary attributes.
answerSummary: Type 1, something you know (password, PIN). Type 2, something you have (smart card, token, phone). Type 3, something you are (fingerprint, iris). Supplementary: somewhere you are (location) and something you do (typing rhythm, signature).
examTrapWarning: MFA requires factors of different types. A password plus a security question is still single-factor.

rows: Smart card, hardware token, authenticator app, security key
Fingerprint, face, iris, retina, palm vein

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Identification and Authentication of People, Devices, and Services
topicName: MFA Factors (Something You Know, Have, Are, Somewhere You Are)
title: Password + PIN is not MFA
prompt: Complete the rule for counting authentication factors.
answerSummary: Two items of the same type (for example a password and a PIN, both things you know) are single-factor authentication. Multifactor requires at least two different factor types.
examTrapWarning: Smart card + PIN is two-factor (have + know). Password + PIN + security question is still one factor.
clozeTemplate: A password plus a PIN is {{c1::single-factor::factor count}} authentication because both are {{c2::something you know::factor type}}. True MFA requires factors of {{c3::different types::rule}}, such as a smart card and a PIN.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Identification and Authentication of People, Devices, and Services
title: Biometric errors: FRR, FAR and CER
prompt: Define FRR and FAR with their error types, and explain CER.
answerSummary: FRR (Type I) rejects a legitimate user, a usability problem. FAR (Type II) accepts an impostor, a security problem. Raising sensitivity lowers FAR and raises FRR. The crossover error rate is where they are equal; a lower CER means a more accurate system.
mnemonic: Type I = I am rejected (insiders annoyed). Type II = Intruder In.
examTrapWarning: Use CER to compare biometric products. FAR is the more dangerous error for high-security areas.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: Lower CER = better device; FAR is the dangerous one.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Identification and Authentication of People, Devices, and Services
title: Why FIDO2 passkeys resist phishing
prompt: Complete the explanation of why FIDO2/WebAuthn resists phishing.
answerSummary: FIDO2 creates a unique key pair per site. The private key never leaves the authenticator, and the browser binds each signature to the real site's origin, so a look-alike phishing domain gets nothing reusable. No shared secret is stored on the server.
examTrapWarning: SMS codes and push approvals can be phished or fatigued; FIDO2 security keys and passkeys are the phishing-resistant MFA answer.
clozeTemplate: FIDO2 / WebAuthn uses a per-site {{c1::public/private key pair::credential type}}. The private key stays on the {{c2::authenticator::device}}, and each signature is bound to the site's {{c3::origin (domain)::binding}}, so credentials captured by a phishing site cannot be replayed.

subdomainName: Federated Identity with a Third-Party Service
title: SAML vs. OAuth 2.0 vs. OpenID Connect
prompt: Contrast SAML 2.0, OAuth 2.0 and OIDC by purpose, token format and typical use.
answerSummary: SAML 2.0: XML assertions for enterprise browser SSO between an IdP and SP (authentication + attributes). OAuth 2.0: delegated authorization via scoped access tokens; it is not an authentication protocol. OIDC: an identity layer on OAuth 2.0 that adds a JWT ID token for authentication; common in modern web and mobile apps.
examTrapWarning: "Let this app read my calendar without my password" is OAuth (authorization). "Sign in with Google" that proves who you are is OIDC.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: SAML and OIDC authenticate; OAuth authorizes.

columns.label: OAuth 2.0
points: API access on a user's behalf

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Federated Identity with a Third-Party Service
topicName: Kerberos (AS, TGS, KDC, Tickets), RADIUS, TACACS+, LDAP
title: Kerberos authentication flow
prompt: Order the steps of a Kerberos logon and service access.
answerSummary: Client authenticates to the Authentication Service and receives a TGT; client presents the TGT to the Ticket Granting Service to request a service ticket; TGS returns the service ticket; client presents it to the target service, which validates it and grants access.
mnemonic: AS gives the TGT; TGS gives the ST; the server grants access.
examTrapWarning: The user's password is never sent across the network. The KDC (AS + TGS) is a single point of failure, and clocks must be in sync (default 5-minute skew).

steps.label: Request to AS
steps.detail: Client sends user ID to the Authentication Service (part of the KDC).

steps.label: AS returns TGT
steps.detail: AS returns a TGT plus session key, encrypted with a key derived from the user's password.

steps.label: Request service ticket
steps.detail: Client sends the TGT and an authenticator to the Ticket Granting Service.

steps.label: TGS returns service ticket
steps.detail: TGS issues a service ticket encrypted with the target service's key.

steps.label: Present ticket to service
steps.detail: Client sends the service ticket and a fresh authenticator to the server.

steps.label: Service grants access
steps.detail: Server decrypts the ticket, validates the timestamp, and allows access.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Federated Identity with a Third-Party Service
topicName: Kerberos (AS, TGS, KDC, Tickets), RADIUS, TACACS+, LDAP
title: Kerberos dependencies
answerSummary: Kerberos runs on port 88, uses symmetric-key cryptography, and relies on synchronized clocks; default tolerated skew is 5 minutes, so NTP outages break authentication.
examTrapWarning: Kerberos uses symmetric keys, not PKI (PKINIT is an optional extension). The KDC is a single point of failure.
clozeTemplate: Kerberos uses {{c1::symmetric::crypto type}} keys and listens on port {{c2::88::port}}. Tickets carry timestamps, so clocks must be synchronized, typically within {{c3::5 minutes::default skew}}; the {{c4::KDC::server}} is a single point of failure.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Federated Identity with a Third-Party Service
topicName: Kerberos (AS, TGS, KDC, Tickets), RADIUS, TACACS+, LDAP
title: RADIUS vs. TACACS+ vs. Diameter
prompt: Contrast RADIUS, TACACS+ and Diameter on transport, encryption and AAA handling.
answerSummary: RADIUS: UDP 1812/1813, encrypts only the password, combines authentication and authorization; common for network and Wi-Fi access. TACACS+: TCP 49, encrypts the entire payload, separates authentication, authorization and accounting; preferred for device administration. Diameter: RADIUS successor over TCP/SCTP with TLS/IPsec, used in mobile and IMS networks.
examTrapWarning: For admin access to routers with per-command authorization and full encryption, choose TACACS+.

contrastData.ruleOfThumb: TACACS+ = TCP, full encryption, separate AAA.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC, Rule-Based, Risk-Based Access Control
title: Access control models
prompt: Compare DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC and rule-based access control: who decides and how.
answerSummary: DAC: the owner sets permissions (ACLs); flexible but Trojan-prone. MAC: the system enforces labels and clearances; non-discretionary. RBAC: permissions follow job roles. ABAC: policies evaluate attributes of subject, object, action and environment. Rule-based: global rules apply to everyone, such as firewall rules.
examTrapWarning: Labels and clearances mean MAC. "Contractors may access only from company devices during business hours" is ABAC.

rows: NTFS file permissions set by the file owner
All nurses can read patient charts
Policy over attributes (user, resource, action, environment)
Managers in EU, on managed device, 9–5

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Manage the Identity and Access Provisioning Lifecycle
topicName: Provisioning, Onboarding, Role Changes, Deprovisioning, Access Reviews
title: Identity and access lifecycle
prompt: Put the identity lifecycle stages in order.
answerSummary: Identity proofing and provisioning at onboarding; ongoing use with periodic access reviews; role change (remove old rights, add new); deprovisioning at termination.
examTrapWarning: Transfers are where privilege creep happens: new rights are added but old ones are not removed.

steps.label: Identity proofing
steps.detail: Verify the person against HR records and identity documents.

steps.label: Provisioning
steps.detail: Create accounts with least-privilege, role-based access.

steps.label: Periodic access review
steps.detail: Managers re-certify access; remove what is no longer needed.

steps.label: Role change (mover)
steps.detail: Revoke old privileges and grant new ones to prevent privilege creep.

steps.label: Deprovisioning (leaver)
steps.detail: Disable accounts promptly at termination; delete after retention period.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Manage the Identity and Access Provisioning Lifecycle
topicName: Provisioning, Onboarding, Role Changes, Deprovisioning, Access Reviews
title: Privilege creep and its fix
prompt: Complete the statement about privilege creep.
answerSummary: Privilege creep is the gradual buildup of access rights as users change jobs without old rights being removed. Periodic access reviews (recertification) by managers, together with RBAC, detect and correct it.
examTrapWarning: Account reviews are the detective control; the root fix is a mover process that removes old access at each transfer.
clozeTemplate: {{c1::Privilege creep::term}} happens when users keep old permissions after changing roles. It violates {{c2::least privilege::principle}} and is caught by periodic {{c3::access reviews (recertification)::control}}.

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

topicName: Privileged Access Management (PAM), Just-in-Time (JIT) Access, Vaulting
title: Privileged access management controls
answerSummary: Just-in-time elevation grants admin rights only when needed and for a limited time. Zero standing privileges means no always-on admin accounts. Credential vaulting stores and rotates privileged passwords and keys. Session recording and monitoring capture privileged activity. Service account governance inventories and rotates non-human credentials.
examTrapWarning: Shared, never-rotated admin passwords are the classic PAM gap. JIT access shrinks the window an attacker can use stolen admin credentials.

rows: Stores privileged secrets; rotates after use
Inventory, ownership and rotation of non-human accounts

references.source: ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide (9th Edition)

subdomainName: Manage the Identity and Access Provisioning Lifecycle
topicName: Provisioning, Onboarding, Role Changes, Deprovisioning, Access Reviews
title: Deprovisioning a hostile leaver
prompt: A database administrator is being dismissed for cause this afternoon. When should their access be removed?
answerSummary: Disable all accounts, VPN, tokens and physical badges at the same time as (or immediately before) the termination meeting, coordinated with HR. Review accounts they created or shared credentials they knew and rotate them.
examTrapWarning: Waiting for the normal monthly account review is too late. Also remember shared and service account passwords the person knew.

heuristicData.technicalReflexTrap: Remove access at the next scheduled account review, or leave accounts active so the DBA can hand over work.
heuristicData.managerAction: Coordinate with HR to revoke all logical and physical access at the moment of notification, then rotate any shared or service credentials the person knew.
heuristicData.governingPrinciple: Deprovisioning must be timely and complete; hostile terminations need immediate, coordinated revocation.
